is.t: The normal distribution (familiarly known as the "bell-shaped curve") is symmetrical, i.e., the mean is halfway between the upper and lower bounds of the 90% confidence interval. When modeling, keep in mind that the normal distribution has a "long tail" -- i.e., the extreme values on either end diminish to increasingly unlikely values, but there is no hard stop. In many modeling scenarios, it may make sense to truncate the normal distribution (for example, it doesn't make sense for > 100% or < 0% of productivity to be lost as a result of a security incident). Use the formula in "Random Value Generator" to generate a random variable with this distribution -- and optionally, apply if / then logic to truncate the upper and/or lower bound for a model that more accurately reflects physical limits. (By default, the chart here shows the "not truncated" normal distribution.)
The histogram is the distribution based on the 10,000 random scenarios from this worksheet.
The "sparklines" are a quick way to visualize the cumulative % and inverse cumulative % curves, respectively.
To recalculate manually -- i.e., to generate 10,000 new random scenarios -- press F9.
